title: Drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
hook: only Luke tells of the angel and the sweat like drops of blood

segments.voice: Yesterday, diakonon: the apostles argued over greatness, and Jesus was among them as one who serves. Your line was servant of the servants of God.

It's late, and the supper is over. Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, to a place Luke says he went as he was accustomed. Somewhere he'd prayed before. A chair by a window, a corner of a church, a walk taken when something is too heavy: some people keep a place like that. He tells the disciples to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he goes on a little further, about a stone's throw, and kneels down.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, AFTER SUPPER.` → `A PLACE HE WENT AS ACCUSTOMED.` → `A STONE'S THROW FURTHER.`

segments.voice: He prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." The chalice is the cup of suffering ahead. He asks honestly for it to pass, then hands the decision over. Then Luke gives two details no other Gospel has: "And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground." Look at the order. The angel comes, and the agony deepens. The angel doesn't take the cup away; the angel helps him drink it. In Luke's picture, strength from heaven isn't an exit. It's company in it. Agony, in Luke's Greek, is agonia, a word that could describe an athlete's strain before a contest, as well as deep anguish. And the sweat is as drops of blood: like. Readers have long debated whether Luke means real blood or heavy, dark drops; the text doesn't settle it. Some early manuscripts of Luke don't have these two verses. The Church receives them as Scripture, and they're in the Latin Vulgate and the Douay. And the disciples? He finds them sleeping for sorrow. Luke is gentle: grief knocked them out. Catholics pray this moment as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden, and some keep a holy hour, remembering that in Matthew and Mark, Jesus asks his friends to watch one hour with him.
screen: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE.` · `AN ANGEL, AND THE AGONY DEEPENS.` · `AGONIA: THE STRAIN BEFORE THE RACE.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `HIS SWEAT AS DROPS OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in a terrible hour right now: a frightening diagnosis, a court date, an addiction, a night in an emergency room, a grief with no bottom. You can't take the cup away, but you can keep watch, staying with them in your mind the way the disciples were asked to. If you pray, ask that they be strengthened, as he was.
Agonia. Luke's word for Jesus' struggle on the Mount of Olives, his sweat like drops of blood, an angel strengthening him to go on. Today's word.
Your line: an angel strengthened him. Not an exit, but company in the hour. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Agony in the Garden as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, and some keep a holy hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, especially on Holy Thursday night.

chat.says: If an angel came to help Jesus in the garden, why was he still in agony?
options: In Luke the angel strengthens him to go on; the agony deepens, and he prays longer.
The angel came to take the cup away, but Jesus sent the angel back to heaven.
The angel came only after the agony was over, to comfort him once it ended.
chat.meaning: Luke says an angel strengthened him, and being in an agony he prayed the longer. Strength from heaven was company in it, not an exit.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer says 'most of us' (narrator speaking for the listener) and drops the uncited 'across a valley'; the narrator's own claim about 'what strength from God can look like' is now framed as Luke's picture; 'many keep a holy hour' softened twice.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 22:42 and 22:43–44.
Manuscript note: 22:43–44 are absent from some early witnesses (e.g., P75, Vaticanus) but present in many others and in the Vulgate; the Church receives them as canonical. Confirm phrasing.
Agonia occurs only here in the New Testament; confirm. Its sense here (athletic strain before a contest vs. anguish) is debated; the teach now gives both.
Holy hour now tied to Matthew 26:40 and Mark 14:37 ('watch one hour'), since Luke has no such line; confirm.
Whether the sweat was actual blood (some link it to hematidrosis) is left open as the text uses 'as'. Confirm.
